q: A volunteer offers one girl private lessons alone at his house. How should this be classed?
o: A safeguarding concern because our own volunteer creates risk
A security issue because the lessons happen without supervision
A safety issue because the house may lack exits
An HR matter because volunteers must follow staff schedules
why: Safeguarding covers harm risked by our own people and activities.

q: Which difference separates safeguarding from child protection?
o: Safeguarding acts before harm for all children at risk
Safeguarding reacts only after harm to one named child
Safeguarding covers only harm happening inside private family homes
Safeguarding replaces all police work whenever children face harm
why: Safeguarding is broader and acts before harm, covering harm caused by us or our work.

q: Staff sign the code, risk assessments precede activities and drivers are vetted. Which pillar is mainly shown?
o: Prevention, because harm is stopped before it can happen
Awareness, because people learn what harm looks like there
Reporting, because concerns are raised through safe channels now
Response, because survivors receive quick and correct action here
why: Risk assessments, codes and vetting are prevention measures.

q: Which action belongs to the Response pillar?
o: Following the policy, escalating the case and never investigating alone
Training new volunteers in induction before they meet any children
Posting reporting channels on every notice board in local languages
Completing activity risk assessments before every single home visit begins
why: Response means acting correctly: follow policy, escalate, and do not investigate alone.

q: A field officer promises registration on a list in return for time with a mother. Which term fits best?
o: Sexual exploitation, because he abuses unequal power for gain
Sexual harassment, because the behaviour occurs between two colleagues
Neglect, because he failed to meet her basic needs
Social safeguard, because he registered families under project rules
why: Exploitation is abuse of unequal power or trust for gain.

q: Which pair is correctly matched?
o: A stolen laptop; a security issue for the organisation
A broken fire exit; a child protection case today
A late vendor payment; a safeguarding concern for children
A teacher hitting pupils; a general safety issue only
why: Theft is security. A teacher hitting pupils is a safeguarding issue.

q: What does 'Do No Harm' require of an organisation?
o: Presence and programmes must never make people less safe
Staff must always answer to donors before affected communities
Projects must avoid all risk of any kind whatsoever
Managers must act only when harm is formally proven
why: Do No Harm means our work must never leave people less safe.

q: Which statement about accountability is correct?
o: Communities know what to expect and can give feedback
Donors alone decide whether a community complaint was valid
Staff report upward but communities are never told anything
Complaints are recorded but no one needs to respond
why: Accountability means being answerable to the people we serve, not only to donors.

q: A supervisor asks a junior colleague for a favour while holding her contract renewal. Why is her yes doubtful?
o: Fear of losing the contract can remove her free choice
Junior staff cannot give consent to any request at work
Contract renewals always require written consent from both senior colleagues
Supervisors automatically lose their authority when they ask for favours
why: Consent is only real when a person is free to say no.

q: Which statement about power is most accurate?
o: Power shifts with context, so one person can hold little or much
Power is fixed by job title, so context never really changes it
Power belongs only to managers, so volunteers and drivers never hold any
Power comes from money alone, so age and gender never really matter
why: Power has many sources and changes with the setting.

q: A driver is alone with a child travelling to an activity. Which safeguard is most direct?
o: Vetted drivers, headcounts and no child alone with drivers
Faster routes, tinted windows and quiet music during trips
Cheaper vendors, longer contracts and no briefings for drivers
Private phones, personal numbers and direct messages with children
why: Vetting, headcounts and never leaving a child alone with a driver reduce the risk.

q: A mother is told her name goes on the list if she spends time with the officer. What is true?
o: Her agreement is not free consent because he controls support
Her agreement is valid consent because she said it aloud
Her agreement is valid consent because she is an adult
Her agreement is valid consent because the offer was optional
why: Control of support removes free choice, so her yes is not consent.

q: What is the purpose of a power map?
o: It shows where harm could happen and safeguards must be strongest
It ranks staff by seniority so managers can set pay bands
It lists donors by funding size so reports can be sorted
It maps office floors so fire exits are easy to find
why: A power map shows who holds power over whom, so safeguards go where risk is highest.

q: Which question is most useful when examining a relationship for power?
o: Who can leave and who would be believed if harm happened?
Who earns the highest salary and holds the longest running contract?
Who speaks the loudest and attends the most weekly staff meetings?
Who owns the vehicle and pays the monthly running fuel costs?
why: Leaving and being believed are the key tests of power in a relationship.

q: Which argument best persuades a leader who says safeguarding costs too much?
o: Prevention costs far less than lost trust, funding and legal liability
Donors will only fund organisations that publish every single incident openly
Staff will accept lower pay when safeguarding rules are very strict
Governments will immediately close organisations that lack a printed policy document
why: The cost of doing nothing is far higher than the cost of prevention.

q: Which cost of doing nothing is the greatest?
o: A child is hurt, which no budget can repair
A donor cuts funding, which no report can repair
A policy expires, which no committee can quickly repair
A brand loses value, which no campaign can repair
why: Harm to a child is the greatest cost.

q: A 12-year-old works long hours as a house help. Which standards apply most directly?
o: ILO Conventions 138 and 182, plus the UNCRC protections
ILO Convention 190 and CEDAW provisions on workplace harassment
IASC principles and the Core Humanitarian Standard on exploitation
IFC Performance Standards and the 2019 OECD donor recommendations
why: Minimum age and worst forms of child labour are covered by ILO 138 and 182 and the UNCRC.

q: A worker says 'I thought she was 18.' What do the IASC principles say?
o: Mistaken belief about age is never a valid defence
Local custom on adulthood decides whether a defence applies
Honest belief reduces the sanction but not the breach
Written proof of age from the girl is enough
why: Principle two says a mistaken belief about age is not a defence.

q: Which IASC principle requires reporting of a colleague's suspected misconduct?
o: Principle five, which requires reporting through proper channels
Principle four, which discourages relationships with aid recipients
Principle three, which bans exchanging aid for favours
Principle six, which holds managers responsible for environment
why: Principle five requires workers to report concerns through proper channels.

q: An aid worker offers a programme place in return for a date. Which principle does this most directly break?
o: Principle three, because it exchanges assistance for sexual favours
Principle two, because it involves a child under eighteen
Principle five, because the worker failed to report staff
Principle four, because a relationship with the recipient formed
why: Principle three bans exchanging assistance for sex or favours.

q: How should an organisation use international standards?
o: Name them in policy and review the policy every two years
Name them in donor reports and update the policy when audited
Replace local policies with them and drop all local rules entirely
Treat them as the maximum and never exceed their stated limits
why: Standards are a minimum that should be named in the policy and reviewed.

q: Which standard sets out freedom from violence and harassment at work?
o: ILO Convention 190, which covers violence and harassment at work
ILO Convention 189, which covers decent work for domestic workers
ILO Convention 182, which covers worst forms of child labour
ILO Convention 138, which covers the minimum age for work
why: ILO 190 deals with violence and harassment at work.

q: A 14-year-old is offered a job in another state and taken from her family. Which law and agency apply?
o: Trafficking in Persons Act, enforced by NAPTIP
Violence Against Persons Act, enforced by police
Cybercrimes Act, enforced by national data regulators
Labour Act, enforced by local employer associations
why: Trafficking is covered by the Trafficking in Persons Act and enforced by NAPTIP.

q: A staff member shares a child's photo online with a real name. Which laws are most relevant?
o: Data Protection Act 2023 and the Child Rights Act
The Labour Act and the Violence Against Persons Act
The Trafficking Act and the Constitution's free movement provisions
Only the Lagos Criminal Law on sexual defilement offences
why: Sharing identifiable images breaks data protection and child rights law.

q: Which agency coordinates the Lagos response to domestic and sexual violence?
o: The Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency, which supports survivors
The Public Defender's office, which licenses private safe houses
The Family Court, which investigates every reported abuse case
The Mirabel Centre, which prosecutes every sexual offence case
why: The DSVA coordinates the response and supports survivors.

q: Why is the gap between law and culture a challenge?
o: Practices like child domestic work stay accepted despite legal limits
Laws are unenforceable and should therefore be ignored in practice
Culture is always harmful and must be rejected by staff
Communities already follow every law so outreach is largely unnecessary
why: Social acceptance can continue even where the law limits a practice.

q: A survivor fears the police process. What is the best practical response?
o: Use trusted referral partners and accompany the survivor throughout
Report to police immediately without asking what she wants
Promise her that the case will certainly end successfully
Close the file because she declined to proceed formally
why: Accompany the survivor, use trusted partners and respect her wishes. Never promise outcomes.

q: Which approach to using the law without being a lawyer is correct?
o: Know the child's legal age and keep a legal referral list
Promise outcomes early so that survivors can feel confident and calm
Share every record widely so lawyers can see the full picture
Avoid the police completely because cases are always mishandled in Lagos
why: Know the basics, keep a referral list and never promise outcomes.

q: A caseworker knows a child has not eaten properly for weeks but records nothing. Which type of harm is this?
o: Neglect, because failing to act on basic needs is harm
Physical abuse, because hunger deliberately causes bodily injury to her
Emotional abuse, because silence always damages the child's growing confidence
Exploitation, because the caseworker clearly gained money from her hunger
why: Failing to meet or act on basic needs is neglect.

q: A manager refuses the travel claims of a staff member who reported his behaviour. How is this best described?
o: Retaliation against a reporter, which is itself abuse of power
A routine finance decision, which is clearly outside safeguarding scope
A performance matter, which should wait for the annual review
A legitimate budget control, which applies equally to all staff
why: Punishing a reporter is retaliation and a misuse of power.

q: Which pattern best describes grooming?
o: Small steps like private contact, gifts and special treatment
A single violent act committed in public by strangers
Open praise given equally to every child at events
Regular supervised lessons run by two trained adult volunteers
why: Grooming starts with small steps such as private contact, gifts and special treatment.

q: A communications officer posts photos of child domestic workers with real names and areas, with no consent. Which label fits best?
o: Digital safeguarding failure and a privacy violation of children
Acceptable promotion because the photos clearly support fundraising goals
Minor policy slip because no physical harm occurred yet
Labour exploitation because the children received no direct payment
why: Posting identifiable images without consent is a digital safeguarding and privacy failure.

q: A community leader pressures a family not to report abuse for reputation. What is this?
o: Obstruction of reporting that can add emotional harm
A respected mediation that protects family honour fairly
A cultural duty that organisations must not question
A private matter outside safeguarding and community concern
why: Blocking a report protects the abuser and adds harm.

q: You notice signs of abuse by a trusted volunteer. What should you do?
o: Report to the safeguarding lead the same day
Confront the volunteer privately and demand an explanation
Wait for more evidence before telling anyone senior
Investigate quietly and interview the child about details
why: Report the same day and never confront or investigate alone.

q: Which set of signs is most associated with exploitation of a child worker?
o: Long working hours, no pay and no freedom to leave
Missing school, looking tired, unwashed and arriving hungry each day
Unexplained injuries, a fear of one adult and sudden withdrawal
Withdrawn behaviour, low confidence and visible anxiety around other adults
why: Exploitation shows as long hours, no pay and no freedom to leave.

q: Which scenario is sexual exploitation under SEAH?
o: Cash distribution made conditional on sexual favours from caregivers
A supervisor mocking a staff member in team meetings
A staff member asking children to wash his car
A communications officer posting photographs without any parental consent
why: Making aid depend on sexual favours is sexual exploitation.

q: Why are child domestic workers at special risk?
o: They depend on employers for food, shelter and pay
They live in organised groups with regular adult supervision
They are well known to police and social workers
They usually choose their work with full family support
why: Dependence on the employer, being hidden and not being believed raise their risk.

q: Before contacting a child domestic worker, what must the team plan for?
o: The child's safety, including the employer's likely angry reaction
The press release, including the programme's expected media coverage
The donor report, including the number of children reached
The staff schedule, including the times of employer meetings
why: Reaching the child can create risk, so plan for her safety first.

q: Which reporting design is safest for child domestic workers?
o: Several routes including a trusted adult outside the household
One route passing through the employer for quick approval
One route passing through village elders for cultural fit
One route using only the staff member's personal phone
why: Offer more than one route, including a trusted adult outside the employer's home.

q: Which is the correct consent practice for child domestic workers?
o: Ask the child and a caregiver in a way allowing refusal
Ask only the employer because the employer legally controls the child
Ask the child once and treat the answer as permanent forever
Ask staff members who know the family well to decide instead
why: Ask the child, not only the employer, in a way that lets them say no.

q: Which set lists the four essential first steps for an organisation?
o: A self-assessment, a budget, essential policies and a named SFP/DSL
Annual report, new logo, office lease and a named auditor
Donor visit, press launch, staff party and a named mascot
Board dinner, website design, fee increase and a named bank
why: Start with a self-assessment, a budget, essential policies and a named SFP/DSL.

q: A policy exists but has no steps, no SEAH provisions and is not shared. How should this be rated?
o: Partial, because it exists but important parts are missing
In place, because a policy document has been written
Not applicable, because policies need not always include SEAH
In place, because staff can request it if needed
why: A policy that exists but lacks key content and sharing is only partially in place.

q: What makes a safeguarding action plan reliable?
o: Every gap has an action, an owner role and a date
Every gap has a wish, an owner name and a hope
Every gap has a report, a donor and a fixed deadline
Every gap has a meeting, a chairperson and a minute book
why: Actions need an owner (a role) and a date, and monthly review.

q: Who should answer self-assessment questions for the most honest picture?
o: Many people, not only managers, answering honestly
Only senior managers, answering for all staff
Only the board, answering from past reports
Only the SFP/DSL, answering from memory alone
why: Ask other people, not only managers, and be honest about gaps.
